body:
Devon Ricci: Dana, Alan — welcome. Dana, thanks for bringing Alan into the conversation. I'm excited to hear more about collections.

Dana Ortiz: Yeah, so quick context for Priya and Devon — since we went live in November on the servicing side, Voxly is handling about fifty-two percent of our inbound. Our CFO is thrilled. She's the one who pushed us to look at collections next.

Alan Weiss: Right. And collections is a totally different beast. It's outbound-heavy, it's compliance-sensitive — TCPA, FDCPA, state-by-state rules — and it's where we have the biggest cost pressure.

Priya Raman: Alan, before we go too deep — what's the primary outcome you'd want from an AI voice agent in collections?

Alan Weiss: Three things. One, first-touch outreach on accounts thirty to sixty days delinquent, which today we do through a dialer with human agents. That's expensive. Two, inbound calls from customers responding to statements or dunning notices — we want to route those intelligently. Three, promise-to-pay setup — capturing the commitment and pushing it into our servicing system.

Devon Ricci: What's the current cost structure on collections?

Alan Weiss: We spend about eighty thousand a month on collections labor, roughly fifteen people plus a supervisor. If we could deflect thirty to forty percent of first-touch outbound to a bot we'd save meaningfully.

Priya Raman: This is exactly what voice_agent_v2 was built for. V2 has outbound campaign support and a TCPA-compliant consent flow — timing windows, do-not-call list checks, and automatic state-rule enforcement. It went GA in December.

Alan Weiss: How do you handle the state rules? Some states you can call before 8 AM, some you can't, some prohibit certain scripts entirely.

Priya Raman: We maintain a state-rules matrix in the platform. When a campaign is set up you designate the account state per contact, and the system enforces the calling windows and script variants automatically. If a state rule blocks a call, it's just skipped and reported.

Alan Weiss: That's better than what we have today, honestly. Our current dialer requires our supervisor to manually configure state windows every morning.

Dana Ortiz: Priya, what does this look like on contract? We're currently at two-forty a year on the two-year term.

Priya Raman: Adding collections would move you to enterprise tier because of the compliance-heavy use case. Enterprise per-minute rate is twelve cents. For your projected collections volume — Alan, what are we talking, twenty thousand outbound attempts a month plus inbound?

Alan Weiss: Roughly. Plus about eight thousand inbound.

Priya Raman: So call it forty-thousand connected minutes on outbound and twenty-four thousand on inbound. At twelve cents that's about seventy-seven hundred a month, so ninety-two K a year on top of your current contract.

Dana Ortiz: What about our current per-minute rate on servicing — does that go up when we move to enterprise tier?

Priya Raman: Good question. If you commit to both lines together I hold servicing at your current fourteen cents through the current term and roll everything into a single enterprise contract at renewal.

Dana Ortiz: I need to see the numbers written down but that structure seems fair.

Alan Weiss: There's one more thing. We may want a fully custom voice — our brand voice is important in collections and generic TTS sounds cold. Do you offer voice cloning?

Priya Raman: We have a custom_voice add-on. It's a one-time twenty-five thousand dollar setup for a licensed brand voice actor, then it's included in the platform fee. Turnaround is about six weeks.

Alan Weiss: I'll think on that. Not a must-have for launch.

Devon Ricci: Alan, one more thing on the compliance side — we can produce audit-ready call recordings and consent logs on demand. That's already in v2.

Alan Weiss: That's essential for us. Regulators can subpoena those at any time.

Devon Ricci: One more thing — for the outbound side, what's your dialer strategy today? Predictive, power, preview?

Alan Weiss: Power dialer. Predictive was too aggressive for our compliance posture.

Priya Raman: V2's outbound engine defaults to preview mode with an option to go power. You'd never touch predictive unless you wanted to.

Alan Weiss: Good.

Dana Ortiz: On the servicing side — we've been really happy with Devon. I want to make sure whoever we get for collections is the same caliber.

Devon Ricci: We can keep me as your CSM across both lines if you want continuity. I've been ramping on collections use cases specifically for this.

Dana Ortiz: I'd prefer that.

Alan Weiss: Same. Continuity matters.

Priya Raman: Done. Devon stays on both.

Alan Weiss: What's the expected timeline from contract signature to first live call on collections?

Marcus Fields: For the outbound campaign side, roughly ten weeks. Inbound routing can start earlier, about six weeks.

Alan Weiss: That works for our August launch target.

Dana Ortiz: Okay. Priya, send us a formal proposal covering the collections expansion. Include the custom voice option priced separately. We want to make a decision by end of May so we can launch in August.

Priya Raman: You'll have it by April twenty-fifth.

Dana Ortiz: Thanks all.

Alan Weiss: Appreciate it.

Devon Ricci: One last logistics thing — I'll set up a kickoff call for the collections implementation the first week of May, assuming signature by end of April.

Alan Weiss: Works. Include our comp lead, Trisha Vaughn.

Devon Ricci: Noted.

Dana Ortiz: Talk soon.
